What you will be able to do

Small numbers, every step shown. Proofs can be skipped; each has a one-sentence summary in the notes.

slides.html:
1. Growth Models

Capital accumulation + diminishing returns
slides.title: 1. Growth Models

slides.html:
Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans

\max\sum\beta^tU(c_t)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ k_{t+1}+c_t=f(k_t)+(1-\delta)k_t
  • Euler equation: U'(c_t)=\beta U'(c_{t+1})[f'(k_{t+1})+1-\delta]
  • Transversality: \lim\beta^tU'(c_t)k_{t+1}=0
  • Steady state (modified golden rule): f'(\bar k)=\dfrac1\beta-1+\delta
slides.title: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans

slides.html:
Worked example: the modified golden rule

\beta=0.96, \delta=0.1, f=k^{1/3}:

f'(\bar k)=\tfrac1\beta-1+\delta=0.1417\ \Rightarrow\ \bar k=3.61,\quad\bar c=1.173

Impatience: optimal capital 3.61 is below the golden-rule 6.09.
slides.title: Worked example: the modified golden rule
Phase Diagram and the Stable Arm

slides.html:
Solving by Log-Linearisation

  • \hat x=\ln(x/\bar x); y=f(x)\Rightarrow\hat y=\dfrac{\bar xf'}{f}\hat x
  • (\hat c,\hat k)_{t+1}=M(\hat c,\hat k)_t, (\lambda_1-1)(\lambda_2-1)<0: saddle
  • Kill the unstable direction z_t=V_{21}\hat c_t+V_{22}\hat k_t=0:
    \hat c_t=-V_{21}^{-1}V_{22}\hat k_t
slides.title: Solving by Log-Linearisation

slides.html:
Worked example: the linearised Ramsey model

Log utility, \beta=0.96, \delta=0.1:

M=\begin{pmatrix}1.029&-0.094\\-0.325&1.042\end{pmatrix},\quad\lambda=0.860,\ 1.211
  • one unstable root, one jump variable ⟹ unique saddle path
  • policy: \hat c=0.558\,\hat k, \hat k'=0.860\,\hat k
  • half-life of a capital gap: 4.6 periods
slides.title: Worked example: the linearised Ramsey model

slides.html:
2. Deterministic Dynamic Programming

Infinite horizon ⟹ recursive problem
slides.title: 2. Deterministic Dynamic Programming

slides.html:
Worked example: a contraction

T(x)=0.5x+1, \beta=0.5, fixed point x=2:

0\to1\to1.5\to1.75\to1.875\to1.9375\dots

The distance to the fixed point halves each step. The Bellman operator does the same with functions.
slides.title: Worked example: a contraction

slides.html:
Properties of the Bellman Equation

V(x)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{F(x,y)+\beta V(y)\}
Assumptions Conclusion
compact continuous constraint + bounded continuous F V exists, unique, continuous
F increasing, \Gamma monotone V increasing
F strictly concave, \Gamma convex V strictly concave, single-valued policy
F differentiable V'(x)=F_x (envelope)
slides.title: Properties of the Bellman Equation

slides.html:
Three Solution Methods

  1. Euler: F_y+\beta V'(y)=0 + envelope V'=F_x ⟹ F_y(x,y)+\beta F_x(y,g(y))=0
  2. Guess and verify: guess V=A\ln k+B, match coefficients
  3. Value-function iteration: v_{i+1}=Tv_i
slides.title: Three Solution Methods

slides.html:
Example: Log Growth (Closed Form)

V(k)=\max_{k'}\ln(k^\alpha-k')+\beta V(k')
A=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha\beta},\qquad k'=\alpha\beta\,k^\alpha

The optimal policy saves a fixed share \alpha\beta of output each period.

Tree cutting: if you will cut, cut tomorrow (waiting a second period is worse).
slides.title: Example: Log Growth (Closed Form)

slides.html:
Worked example: iteration and the closed form

V_n=A_n\ln k+B_n, A_{n+1}=\alpha(1+\beta A_n), \alpha=\tfrac13, \beta=0.96:

0.333,\ 0.440,\ 0.474,\ 0.485,\ 0.489\ \to\ \tfrac\alpha{1-\alpha\beta}=0.490

Saving rate \alpha\beta=0.32: k_0=1\to0.32\to0.219\to0.193\to\bar k=0.181.
slides.title: Worked example: iteration and the closed form

slides.html:
3. Stochastic Dynamic Programming

Replace tomorrow's value by a conditional expectation
slides.title: 3. Stochastic Dynamic Programming

slides.html:
Markov Chains and the Stochastic Euler Equation

  • \psi_t=(P')^t\psi_0; stationary \psi^*=P'\psi^*
  • V(x,z)=\sup\{F+\beta E[V(y,z')|z]\}; no steady-state point, only a stationary distribution
  • Stochastic growth:
    U'(c_t)=\beta E_t\Big[U'(c_{t+1})\big(z_{t+1}f'(k_{t+1})+1-\delta\big)\Big]
slides.title: Markov Chains and the Stochastic Euler Equation

slides.html:
Worked example: a Markov chain forgets its start

P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.2&0.8\end{pmatrix}, start in state 1:

t 0 1 2 3 4 \infty
\Pr(state 1) 1 0.9 0.83 0.781 0.747 \tfrac23

Durations 10 and 5 periods ⟹ stationary shares \tfrac23,\tfrac13.
slides.title: Worked example: a Markov chain forgets its start

slides.html:
4. Labour Markets and Search

Unemployment as an investment
slides.title: 4. Labour Markets and Search

slides.html:
Worked example: a reservation wage

Offers U[0,2], b=0.5, \beta=0.95:

\bar w=0.5+4.75(2-\bar w)^2\ \Rightarrow\ \bar w=1.53
  • accept w.p. 0.233; expected spell 4.3 periods
  • b=1: \bar w=1.63, accept 18%

Generous benefits make workers choosier.
slides.title: Worked example: a reservation wage

slides.html:
Comparative Statics and Variants

  • b\uparrow,\ \beta\uparrow,\ F\to G\le F,\ more dispersion ⟹ \bar w\uparrow
  • Firing risk: \bar w=b+\frac\beta{1-\beta(1-\delta)}\int(w-\bar w)dF ⟹ \bar w\downarrow
  • Wage growth g: value of accepting \frac{w}{1-\beta(1+g)}
  • Changing environment: \bar w(G)\ne\bar w(B)
slides.title: Comparative Statics and Variants

slides.html:
DMP: Matching, Free Entry, Nash Bargaining

  • Matching M(u,v), \theta=v/u, f(\theta)=M/u, q(\theta)=f/\theta
  • u=\dfrac\delta{\delta+f(\theta)} (Beveridge curve)
  • Free entry V=0 ⟹ tightness curve w=z-(1-\beta(1-\delta))\dfrac{kz}{\beta q(\theta)}
  • Nash bargaining ⟹ wage curve w=(1-\phi)b+\phi(1+k\theta)z
slides.title: DMP: Matching, Free Entry, Nash Bargaining

slides.html:
Worked example: DMP in numbers

z=1, b=0.4, \phi=0.5, \delta=0.1, k=0.3, f=0.5\sqrt\theta:

Quantity Value
tightness \theta 1.30
wage w 0.895
job-finding f / vacancy-filling q 57% / 44%
unemployment u / vacancies v 14.9% / 19.4%
slides.title: Worked example: DMP in numbers

slides.html:
5. Complete Markets and Welfare Theorems

Insurance for every state
slides.title: 5. Complete Markets and Welfare Theorems

slides.html:
Arrow–Debreu and Risk Sharing

  • Trade contingent claims once; FOC \beta^tU'(C_t^i)\pi(S^t)=\mu^ip_t^0(S^t)
  • Dividing across agents ⟹ U'(C^i)/U'(C^j)=\mu^i/\mu^j (constant)
C_t^i(S^t)=\tilde\mu^iY_t(S^t)

Each consumes a fixed share of aggregate consumption: individual risk is fully shared ⟹ a representative household.

Prices: p_t^0(S^t)=\beta^t\dfrac{U'(Y_t)}{U'(Y_0)}\pi(S^t|S_0)p_0^0
slides.title: Arrow–Debreu and Risk Sharing

slides.html:
Worked example: risk sharing

Aggregate (3,1); agent 1 has (2,1), agent 2 has (1,0); log utility.

  • state prices p_H=\tfrac16, p_L=\tfrac12
  • PV: \tfrac56 and \tfrac16 ⟹ shares \tfrac56,\tfrac16
  • c^1=(2.5,0.83), c^2=(0.5,0.17)

Fixed shares of the aggregate, whatever the state.
slides.title: Worked example: risk sharing

slides.html:
Sequential Markets and Welfare Theorems

  • Arrow-security price: \tilde q_t(S^t,S')=\beta\dfrac{U'(Y_{t+1})}{U'(Y_t)}\pi(S'|S^t)=\dfrac{p^0_{t+1}}{p^0_t}
  • Equivalence: discount and add + No-Ponzi ⟹ same lifetime budget
  • First Welfare Theorem: AD equilibrium is Pareto efficient
  • Planner \max\sum\lambda^i\beta^tU(C^i): C^i=\tilde\lambda^iY ⟹ solve equilibrium via the planner
slides.title: Sequential Markets and Welfare Theorems

slides.html:
6. Asset Pricing

The SDF: today's value of a unit of future consumption
slides.title: 6. Asset Pricing

slides.html:
The Lucas Tree

P_t=\beta E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+1})}{U'(d_t)}(P_{t+1}+d_{t+1})\Big],\quad Q_t=\beta E_t\Big[\frac{U'(d_{t+1})}{U'(d_t)}\Big]
  • SDF M_{t,t+1}=\beta\dfrac{U'(C_{t+1})}{U'(C_t)}
  • Forward iteration: P_t=\sum_{\tau>t}E_t[\beta^{\tau-t}\frac{U'(d_\tau)}{U'(d_t)}d_\tau] (no bubbles)
slides.title: The Lucas Tree

slides.html:
Worked example: pricing a tree

Log utility ⟹ P=\tfrac\beta{1-\beta}d=24\,d whatever the risk.

d'\in\{0.9,1.1\} from d=1: Q=0.9697, R^f=1.0313; stock return mean 1.0417 ⟹ premium \approx1\%.
slides.title: Worked example: pricing a tree

slides.html:
Term Structure

  • Q_{2t}=\beta^2E_t[U'(d_{t+2})/U'(d_t)]; YTM_j=R_{t,t+j}^{1/j}
  • Expectations hypothesis generally fails (risk term)
  • Inverted yield curve ⟹ low expected future consumption ⟹ often a recession signal
slides.title: Term Structure

slides.html:
C-CAPM and the Equity Premium Puzzle

E[R]-\bar R=-\bar R\,\mathrm{cov}(M,R),\qquad\Big|\frac{E[R-\bar R]}{\sigma_R}\Big|\le\frac{\sigma(M)}{E[M]}

Lognormal + CRRA: \ln(1+\bar r)-\ln(1+\bar r^f)=\gamma\,\mathrm{cov}(\epsilon_c,\epsilon_r). Data: premium 6%, covariance 0.002 ⟹ \gamma\approx30.
slides.title: C-CAPM and the Equity Premium Puzzle

slides.html:
Worked example: the size of the puzzle

Premium =\gamma\cdot\operatorname{cov}(\epsilon_c,\epsilon_r):

  • \gamma=1: 0.002 = 0.2%
  • data: 6% ⟹ \gamma=0.06/0.002=30

With \gamma=30 a 50–50 bet doubling or cutting wealth by 20% has a certainty equivalent of 0.82.
slides.title: Worked example: the size of the puzzle

slides.html:
7. Consumption Theory

Smoothing, not hoarding
slides.title: 7. Consumption Theory

slides.html:
The Permanent-Income Hypothesis

  • R=1/\beta ⟹ U'(c_t) is a martingale; quadratic utility ⟹ c_t=E_t c_{t+1}
  • Lifetime budget + martingale:
    c_t=r\,a_{t-1}+\frac r{1+r}E_t\sum_j\frac{y_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}
  • Saving =-E_t\sum_{j\ge1}\dfrac{\Delta y_{t+j}}{(1+r)^j}; \Delta c reflects only revisions of income expectations
slides.title: The Permanent-Income Hypothesis

slides.html:
Worked example: how much of a windfall is spent?

r=5\%, income +1:

Persistence \rho Consumption rises by
0 (one-off) 0.048
0.5 0.091
1 (permanent) 1
slides.title: Worked example: how much of a windfall is spent?

slides.html:
Precautionary Saving

  • Prudence U'''>0 ⟹ U' convex ⟹ E[U'(Ra_1+y_1)]>U'(Ra_1)
  • Income risk (mean-preserving spread) ⟹ saving rises
  • Quadratic utility U'''=0 ⟹ no precautionary saving (certainty equivalence)
slides.title: Precautionary Saving

slides.html:
Worked example: a buffer

U=\ln c, R=\beta=1, y_0=2, y_1\in\{1,3\}:

\tfrac1{2-a}=\tfrac12\Big(\tfrac1{1+a}+\tfrac1{3+a}\Big)\ \Rightarrow\ 2a^2+4a-1=0,\ a=0.225

Quadratic utility (U'''=0): saving 0.
slides.title: Worked example: a buffer

slides.html:
8. Incomplete Markets and Heterogeneity

Precautionary saving + borrowing constraints
slides.title: 8. Incomplete Markets and Heterogeneity

slides.html:
Why r<1/\beta-1

  • complete markets: r=1/0.96-1=4.17\%
  • incomplete markets: even at R\beta=1 everyone saves a buffer
  • so at R=1/\beta saving exceeds investment ⟹ price of saving must fall

Aiyagari: r<4.17\%; more risk, lower r.
slides.title: Why r<1/\beta-1

slides.html:
Numerical Algorithms

Shooting (Huggett / Aiyagari)

  1. guess q (or r)
  2. solve the household problem
  3. find the invariant distribution \mu
  4. compute excess demand; adjust price; iterate

Krusell–Smith

  1. guess \ln K'=a_z+b_z\ln K
  2. solve the individual problem
  3. simulate a panel, compute K_t
  4. regress to update (a,b); iterate; check R^2
slides.title: Numerical Algorithms

slides.html:
Overlapping Generations (Diamond)

  • Two-period lives; S_t=(1+n)k_{t+1}
  • Log + CD: k_{t+1}=\dfrac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{(1+\beta)(1+n)}k_t^\alpha
  • Equilibrium need not be efficient: f'(k)<n is dynamic inefficiency
slides.title: Overlapping Generations (Diamond)

slides.html:
Worked example: OLG efficiency

Log utility, n=0, full depreciation:

\alpha \beta k^* f'(k^*) verdict
1/3 0.6 0.125 1.33 efficient
0.2 1 0.318 0.50 inefficient

Inefficient ⟹ a pay-as-you-go pension makes every generation better off.
slides.title: Worked example: OLG efficiency

slides.html: 9. Solving Linear Dynamic Systems
slides.title: 9. Solving Linear Dynamic Systems

slides.html:
Blanchard–Kahn

A\begin{pmatrix}E_ty_{t+1}\\x_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}=B\begin{pmatrix}y_t\\x_t\end{pmatrix}+G\epsilon_t

y_t: n jump variables; k = number of eigenvalues with |\lambda|>1: k=n unique; k<n multiple; k>n none.

Solve the unstable block forward with T_t=V_{nn}y_t+V_{nm}x_t (transversality):

y_t=-V_{nn}^{-1}V_{nm}x_t-\cdots
slides.title: Blanchard–Kahn

slides.html:
Worked example: checking the linearisation

x=1.01\bar x, y=0.98\bar y, z=x^2/y:

  • rule: \hat z=2(0.01)-(-0.02)=0.04; exact 1.0409 ✓

Counting roots (one jump variable):

Roots Verdict
0.8,\ 1.3 unique
0.8,\ 0.9 indeterminate
1.2,\ 1.3 no solution
slides.title: Worked example: checking the linearisation

slides.html:
10. Real Business Cycles

Cycles as the optimal response to technology shocks
slides.title: 10. Real Business Cycles

slides.html:
The RBC Model

  • U=\ln c+\theta\ln(1-N); Y=ak^\alpha(XN)^{1-\alpha}; \ln a_t=\rho\ln a_{t-1}+e_t
  • Labour–leisure: \lambda(1-\alpha)aK^\alpha N^{-\alpha}=\dfrac\theta{1-N}
  • Euler: \lambda_t\gamma=\beta E_t[\lambda_{t+1}(\alpha a k^{\alpha-1}N^{1-\alpha}+1-\delta)]
  • Positive shock ⟹ wages↑ ⟹ intertemporal substitution: work and invest more
slides.title: The RBC Model

slides.html:
Worked example: an RBC steady state

Quarterly: \alpha=\tfrac13, \beta=0.99, \delta=0.025:

  • k/y=\alpha/(1/\beta-1+\delta)=9.5 quarters
  • i/y=\delta k/y=0.2375, c/y=0.76
  • \rho=0.95: the shock fades slowly
slides.title: Worked example: an RBC steady state

slides.html:
Decentralisation

  • Households own capital: Tobin's q=\mu/\lambda, invest when q>1
  • Firms own capital: shareholders' SDF discounts profits
  • Constant returns ⟹ both decentralisations coincide with the planner
slides.title: Decentralisation

slides.html: 11. Money and the Classical Dichotomy
slides.title: 11. Money and the Classical Dichotomy

slides.html:
The Classical Dichotomy

  • Real variables: \hat y_t=\dfrac{1+\phi}{\alpha+\phi+\sigma(1-\alpha)}a_t (independent of nominal variables)
  • Nominal variables not pinned down: need a policy rule
  • Fisher: \hat i_t=\hat r_t+E_t\hat\pi_{t+1}

Rule i=\phi_\pi\pi+\epsilon: \phi_\pi>1 (Taylor principle) ⟹ unique price path.
slides.title: The Classical Dichotomy

slides.html:
Worked example: neutral money

\sigma=\phi=1, \alpha=\tfrac13: \hat y=\dfrac{1+\phi}{\alpha+\phi+\sigma(1-\alpha)}a=a

A 1% technology shock raises output 1%, whatever the central bank does.
slides.title: Worked example: neutral money

slides.html:
Worked example: the Taylor principle

\hat\pi_t=\tfrac1{\phi_\pi}E_t\hat\pi_{t+1}+\tfrac1{\phi_\pi}u_t:

  • \phi_\pi=1.5, one-period shock u_0=1: \hat\pi_0=0.667, then 0: unique
  • \phi_\pi=0.8: coefficient 1.25>1, forward solution diverges: many paths
slides.title: Worked example: the Taylor principle

slides.html:
Money in Utility and the Friedman Rule

  • U_M=U_C\dfrac i{1+i}: price of holding cash is 1-Q=\dfrac i{1+i}
  • Money demand: \hat m-\hat p=\frac\sigma v\hat y-\frac1{v(1-\beta)}\hat i; real variables unchanged (neutrality)
  • Friedman rule: i^*=0 ⟹ E\pi=-r<0 (deflation)
slides.title: Money in Utility and the Friedman Rule

slides.html:
Worked example: the Friedman rule

\beta=0.96: real rate 4.17\%. Set i=0 ⟹ inflation =-4.17\% a year: cash earns the same real return as bonds.
slides.title: Worked example: the Friedman rule

slides.html:
12. The New Keynesian Model

Monopolistic competition + sticky prices
slides.title: 12. The New Keynesian Model

slides.html:
Monopolistic Competition (Dixit–Stiglitz)

  • C=\big[\int C_j^{\frac{\theta-1}\theta}dj\big]^{\frac\theta{\theta-1}}; demand C_j=(P_j/P)^{-\theta}C
  • Price = markup × marginal cost: \dfrac{P_j}P=\dfrac\theta{\theta-1}\varphi
  • Flexible prices: \hat y^f=\dfrac{1+\eta}{\eta+\sigma}\hat z; natural rate \hat r^f=\sigma E[\hat y^f_{t+1}-\hat y^f_t]
slides.title: Monopolistic Competition (Dixit–Stiglitz)

slides.html:
Calvo Pricing: NKPC and IS

\hat p_j=(1-\omega\beta)\sum(\omega\beta)^i(\hat p_{t+i}+\hat\varphi_{t+i})
\pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t,\quad x_t=E_tx_{t+1}-\tfrac1\sigma(i_t-E_t\pi_{t+1}-r^f_t)

\kappa=\dfrac{(1-\omega)(1-\omega\beta)(\eta+\sigma)}\omega: stickier prices, smaller \kappa.
slides.title: Calvo Pricing: NKPC and IS
Worked example: the slope of the Phillips curve

slides.html:
Worked example: determinacy

\tilde\kappa=0.172: (1-\beta)/\tilde\kappa=0.058.

\phi_\pi,\ \phi_x \phi_\pi+0.058\phi_x Verdict
1.5, 0.5 1.53 determinate
0.9, 1.5 0.987 indeterminate
slides.title: Worked example: determinacy

slides.html: 13. Optimal Monetary Policy
slides.title: 13. Optimal Monetary Policy

slides.html:
The Divine Coincidence

  • No cost-push shock: i_t=r_t^f+\phi_\pi\pi_t (\phi_\pi>1) ⟹ \pi=x=0
  • Stabilising inflation and the gap do not conflict
  • Wicksellian rate i=r^f
slides.title: The Divine Coincidence

slides.html:
Cost-Push Shocks: Discretion vs Commitment

\min\ \tfrac12E\sum\beta^i(\pi^2+\lambda x^2)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \pi_t=\beta E\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t+e_t
  • Discretion: \pi_t=-\frac\lambda\kappa x_t; x=-\frac{\kappa}{\lambda+\kappa^2}e, \pi=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\kappa^2}e
  • Commitment: \pi_t=-\frac\lambda\kappa(x_t-x_{t-1}) — cares about the change in the gap
slides.title: Cost-Push Shocks: Discretion vs Commitment

slides.html:
Worked example: discretion vs commitment

\kappa=0.2, \lambda=0.1, one-off shock e_0=1:

x_0 \pi_0 afterwards loss
Discretion -1.43 0.71 0 0.357
Commitment -1.08 0.54 gap <0, \pi<0 0.269

Commitment promises below-target inflation later; time-inconsistent.
slides.title: Worked example: discretion vs commitment
The Value of Commitment and Time Inconsistency

slides.html: 14. Looking Back
slides.title: 14. Looking Back

slides.html:
Map of Models

Model Market structure Key result
Solow / Ramsey planner steady state, saddle path, Euler
McCall / DMP frictions reservation wage; tightness & wage curves
Arrow–Debreu complete markets risk sharing; SDF pricing
PIH one asset consumption martingale; precautionary saving
Huggett / Aiyagari / K–S incomplete markets r<1/\beta-1; distributions matter
RBC competitive cycles as optimal response
New Keynesian sticky prices NKPC / IS; Taylor principle; commitment
slides.title: Map of Models

slides.html:
Ideas to Take Away

  • Euler equation + transversality are the "Newton's laws" of dynamic macro
  • Contraction mapping: recursive problems have a solution, unique and computable
  • Complete markets ⟹ representative household; incomplete ⟹ distributions matter
  • The SDF unifies pricing; risk premium = covariance with the SDF
  • Blanchard–Kahn: jump variables = unstable roots ⟺ unique equilibrium ⟺ Taylor principle
  • Nominal stickiness gives monetary policy real effects; expectations make policy powerful

References: Ljungqvist–Sargent; Stokey–Lucas–Prescott; Romer; Galí; Walsh.
slides.title: Ideas to Take Away

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
Solow saving is optimal exogenous; Ramsey has less capital than the golden rule
Poor countries always catch up only conditional convergence
Equity premium puzzle = mispricing simple C-CAPM needs \gamma\approx30
Precautionary saving needs risk aversion needs prudence, U'''>0
Incomplete markets leave r unchanged r<1/\beta-1
Blanchard–Kahn finds a solution counts roots: unstable = jump
Taylor principle: raise rates a lot raise the real rate: more than one-for-one
slides.title: Common misconceptions
